intro: A rocking phrase in B minor grows into great repeated chords, then returns as quietly as a memory. La Pianista plays this Prelude from Rachmaninoff’s last set of thirteen.

sections.label: A · Rocking notes and held chords
sections.mNote: Short triplet figures lean against sustained chords

sections.label: B · Heavy chords over low F♯
sections.mNote: Pesante: repeated chords build above the bass

sections.label: C · Long notes and quick runs
sections.mNote: The piano softens; runs curl around sustained notes

sections.label: A′ · The rocking phrase returns
sections.mNote: A tempo, come prima restores the first phrase

sections.label: Coda · Low B and final chords
sections.mNote: The bass reaches down beneath the last held chord

cues.title: A phrase that rocks
cues.text: Short triplet figures rock against long, tied chords. Both hands speak together in B minor, then leave a little silence before answering. The marking is Lento, and the first phrase stays close to the middle of the piano.
cues.evidence: Gutheil first edition (1911), p. 40, opening systems: Lento, triplet figures, tied chords and rests. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/e0/IMSLP105591-PMLP02018-Rachmaninov_-_32_-_13_Preludes_(ed.Gutheil).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Heavy chords, deep F♯
cues.text: Pesante — heavy. The piano repeats its chords over a deep F♯, and the short rocking rhythm begins to thunder. A crescendo carries it towards the broad, two-handed chords of Tempo I.
cues.evidence: Gutheil first edition, pp. 40–41: pesante over low F♯, poco a poco cresc. and the fortissimo Tempo I passage.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Rachmaninoff’s favourite prelude
cues.text: Arnold Böcklin’s painting The Return lies behind this Prelude. Rachmaninoff tells the pianist Benno Moiseiwitsch that it is his favourite of his preludes.
cues.evidence: The painting connection and Rachmaninoff’s statement to Moiseiwitsch are recorded in the work’s reception history: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preludes,_Op._32_(Rachmaninoff). The account comes through Moiseiwitsch’s later recollection.

cues.title: Long notes above the runs
cues.text: After the repeated chords, the piano returns to pp. Long upper notes hang over quieter chords; small runs gather around them, growing from groups of six and seven notes into a rapid sweep across the keyboard.
cues.evidence: Gutheil first edition, pp. 42–43: L’istesso tempo, pp, then six- and seven-note groups and the veloce passage.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The first phrase comes home
cues.text: A tempo, come prima — at the tempo, as before. After the long runs, the opening’s rocking notes and tied chords return in B minor. The hands come close together again.
cues.evidence: Gutheil first edition, p. 43: the fermata after the rising run, followed by a tempo, come prima and the opening phrase.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The piano reaches down
cues.text: The closing phrases reach into the low bass, with little flourishes above them. A final B lies far below the held chord. Rachmaninoff marks the ending pp and lets the fermata hold it open.
cues.evidence: Gutheil first edition, p. 43, final two systems: descending bass, closing flourishes, low B and the final pp fermata.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The rocking rhythm turns heavy
transitions.from: A · Rocking notes and held chords
transitions.to: B · Heavy chords over low F♯
transitions.how: A low F♯, the dominant of B minor, holds beneath repeated chords marked pesante. The opening’s triplet rhythm persists as the chords climb and grow. At Tempo I, both hands fill out the piano in fortissimo.
transitions.evidence: Gutheil first edition, pp. 40–41: pesante, F♯ pedal, crescendo and Tempo I.

transitions.title: The chords stop pressing forward
transitions.from: B · Heavy chords over low F♯
transitions.to: C · Long notes and quick runs
transitions.how: The repeated piano chords slow and diminish to a fermata. L’istesso tempo follows at pp, with long upper notes over widely separated bass notes. Small runs begin to fill the space between the chords.
transitions.evidence: Gutheil first edition, pp. 41–42: rit. e dim., fermata, then L’istesso tempo at pp.

transitions.title: A rising run releases the opening
transitions.from: C · Long notes and quick runs
transitions.how: The piano’s rapid figures climb, diminish and pause under a fermata. A tempo, come prima brings back the rocking phrase in B minor. The hands leave their wide-ranging runs and return to the joined chords of the opening.
transitions.evidence: Gutheil first edition, p. 43, first three systems: rising run, diminuendo, fermata and a tempo, come prima.

transitions.title: The last bass notes descend
transitions.to: Coda · Low B and final chords
transitions.how: The returning phrase breaks into shorter exchanges. Low bass notes descend beneath the piano’s little flourishes, ending on B below the last held chord. The final marking is pp, with a fermata.
transitions.evidence: Gutheil first edition, p. 43, final two systems: descending bass, widely spaced final chord and pp fermata.

composer.epithet: In exile he earned his living at the piano, while the bells of his Russian childhood kept sounding through the music he wrote.
facts: Zverev and Siloti at the piano; Taneyev and Arensky in composition
Ivanovka, Dresden, New York, Villa Senar and Beverly Hills
Four piano concertos, three symphonies, three completed operas, choral music, songs and piano works

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Rachmaninoff to Leonard Liebling, 1939; published in The Musical Courier, 5 April 1943

composer.background:
“My hearty thanks to the old man for not having forgotten about me!” Rachmaninoff wrote to the singer Mikhail Slonov on 26 December 1892. The old man was Tchaikovsky, who had praised his opera Aleko in a newspaper interview. Rachmaninoff was nineteen, newly graduated from the Moscow Conservatory with its Great Gold Medal. Tchaikovsky helped get the opera into the Bolshoi, and in May 1893 sat in the audience applauding. For a young composer, it was an excellent beginning.

His childhood had been less orderly. Born into a landowning family, he grew up at Oneg, near Novgorod, until his father’s financial failures forced a move to St Petersburg. He entered the Conservatory there in 1883. His parents separated; his sister Sofia died of diphtheria; schoolwork went badly. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where he heard the voices and bells that would stay with him. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended a move to Moscow, under the formidable care of the piano teacher Nikolai Zverev.
